page: Amazon Web Services g4ad.2xlarge is a GPU-accelerated instance powered by an AMD EPYC 7R32 processor with an x86_64 architecture. It features 8 vCPUs, consisting of 4 physical cores with 2 threads per core, running at a clock speed of 3.0 GHz. The system is equipped with 32.0 GB of DDR4 memory, providing 4.0 GB of RAM per core. Graphics processing is handled by a single AMD Radeon Pro Navi V520 GPU with 8 GB of VRAM. Storage is bundled with 300 GB of local NVMe SSD capacity, and network connectivity is delivered via a baseline bandwidth of 4 Gbps under the Nitro hypervisor.

Performance benchmarks indicate moderate capabilities across general computing tasks, with Geekbench single-core and multi-core scores landing in the average tier. However, the instance exhibits notable performance constraints in raw compute and memory throughput. The stress-ng single-core CPU performance is positioned in the bottom 10%, while multi-core CPU performance and large-block memory read and write bandwidth fall into the bottom 25%. LLM inference tasks also show limitations, with prompt processing for a medium 7B model rated in the bottom 10%.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the g4ad.2xlarge offers a balanced resource density for workloads requiring dedicated GPU acceleration without the premium cost of high-end enterprise accelerators. The integrated 300 GB NVMe SSD provides fast local storage, though the lower network baseline of 4 Gbps and weak multi-core scaling present clear tradeoffs. This instance is best suited for graphics-intensive applications, remote workstation hosting, image processing, and lightweight GPU-accelerated tasks rather than heavy LLM inference or high-throughput database operations.
description: Amazon Web Services g4ad.2xlarge is a GPU-accelerated instance featuring an AMD EPYC 7R32 processor with 8 vCPUs, 32.0 GB of DDR4 RAM, and a dedicated AMD Radeon Pro Navi V520 GPU with 8 GB of VRAM. Built on the Nitro hypervisor, it includes 300 GB of local NVMe SSD storage and a 4 Gbps baseline network bandwidth. Benchmark data shows average performance in Geekbench single-core and multi-core tests, alongside moderate results in image processing and software compilation. However, it exhibits performance tradeoffs, including weak large-block memory bandwidth and poor single-core stress-ng CPU performance. Qualitatively, the instance provides a cost-effective entry point for GPU-accelerated workloads that do not demand high-end enterprise compute. It is well-suited for graphics-intensive applications, remote workstations, and lightweight GPU tasks.
